Maine Senate Confirms Vaughan Woodruff as Chair of the State Workforce Development Board

October 5, 2026

For Immediate Release

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Senate confirmed Vaughan Woodruff, principal of EquinoxDG, to a second term as chair of the State Workforce Development Board (SWDB). Gov. Janet Mills announced her nomination of Woodruff on Sept. 8, 2026. Woodruff has served as chair of the SWDB since 2023.

Prior to founding EquinoxDG, Woodruff was vice president of regulatory reform at the Interstate Renewable Energy Council and vice president of workforce development and interconnection strategy at ReVision Energy, where he oversaw the company's long-term strategic vision for training and talent development and developed nationally recognized registered apprenticeships in clean energy.

"The State Workforce Development Board plays a critical role in coordinating Maine's workforce development efforts to support economic growth and address workforce challenges," said Maine Department of Labor Commissioner Laura Fortman. "Vaughan Woodruff is a well-respected business leader with deep workforce expertise. His continued leadership will help maintain momentum as we strengthen Maine's workforce and economy."

"I appreciate the trust that Gov. Mills and the Maine Senate have placed in me through my nomination and confirmation to continue serving the people of Maine in this role," said Woodruff. "I feel privileged to work with the outstanding staff and members of the Board to increase the accessibility of the workforce system to Maine workers and businesses and to proactively address the workforce challenges ahead of us."

Woodruff is a seventh-generation Maine native who was raised in Pittsfield. He earned a bachelor's degree in civil engineering from the University of Maine and a master's degree in education from Prescott College in Arizona. Woodruff was the founder and CEO of Insource Renewables, an employee-owned solar company that was recognized as a Best for the World for Workers company by B Lab prior to its acquisition by ReVision Energy in 2021.

During Woodruff's tenure as chair, the SWDB has:

  • Launched Work Source Maine, the state's online resource connecting job seekers, students, parents, educators, career counselors and employers with resources to explore, plan and achieve career and workforce goals;

  • Launched the Maine Workforce Pell program, which expands federal Pell Grant eligibility to approved short-term, career-focused training programs that deliver industry-recognized credentials and measurable employment results, preparing students for in-demand occupations; and

  • Secured $15M+ in funding to support industry partnerships in advanced manufacturing, forest bioproducts and defense, and expand career exploration, job supports, and upskilling investments including registered pre-apprenticeships

As chair, Woodruff will continue to work with the SWDB, state agencies, education and training providers, employers and other partners to strengthen Maine's workforce development system and help connect Maine people with career opportunities.

Woodruff serves on the Electrical Technologies Advisory Committee at Kennebec Valley Community College and previously served on the Western Mountains Committee of the Maine Community Foundation and the Pittsfield Planning Board. Woodruff lives in Pittsfield with his wife, Holly Zadra, and their two sons, Eamon and Goran.

AUGUSTA, MAINE – Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today traveled to Brunswick Town Hall to mark the start of in-person, no-excuse absentee voting in Maine today. 

“Maine is always a national leader in voter turnout, and we saw record turnout in the June primary. In person absentee voting – Maine’s version of early voting – is part of the special sauce that makes voting convenient to the citizenry and drives up turnout,” said Secretary Bellows. “Anyone can vote early for any reason starting today until October 29, and there are lots of ways to vote absentee – in person, by mail or utilizing a secure ballot drop box.”

This week, voters who are not able to make it to the polls on Election Day or who simply wish to avoid the crowds can begin casting absentee ballots, either in-person at their local town hall or by mailing back their signed and sealed ballot or dropping it in a local secure ballot box. As of Friday, October 2, more than 70,000 Mainers had requested an absentee ballot. Absentee ballot reports are posted on Tuesdays and Thursdays on the Secretary of State’s website.  

Brunswick Town Clerk Fran Smith joined Secretary Bellows to talk about the tasks and challenges that face local election officials this election cycle and why Mainers can expect business as usual for the November 3 General Election.

“This is a busy but exciting time for our office, as I know it is for towns across the state,” said Brunswick Town Clerk Fran Smith. “Our local staff, as well as volunteers on Election Day, are so incredibly vital to ensuring everything runs smoothly right up through the counting of the ballots after the polls close on Election Day.”

As absentee voting gets underway, Secretary Bellows urged voters to make a plan to ensure their ballots are returned by close of polls on Election Day. In Maine, only those ballots received by close of polls are counted, regardless of postmark. Maine offers an online absentee ballot tracking service for voters to track the status of their absentee ballot to be sure that the clerk has received and accepted the ballot. If a voter’s ballot has not been received by Election Day, voters may go in person to the polls on November 3 to request that the missing absentee ballot be rejected or cancelled and cast a vote in person.

“The election should be business as usual this year because the election laws haven’t changed, but sometimes life gets in the way. We have all unfortunately experienced frustration with the postal service and things from everyday mail to prescriptions not arriving in a timely manner,” Secretary Bellows said. “That’s why it can be so helpful to vote early.”

“It’s exciting – Election Day will be here before we know it, and now is the time to make your voting plan,” she said.

items.content_html:
Oct 05, 2026

Reminds Maine people and visitors ticks remain active even as temperatures fall

As days get shorter and leaves begin to change, ticks remain active across Maine. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) urges all Maine people and visitors to protect themselves from tick bites this fall.

Ticks can be active throughout the fall and during winter days, whenever temperatures rise above freezing. Fall is a busy time for outdoor activities, bringing people into contact with ticks more often. People may encounter them during everyday fall activities, like cleaning the yard or hunting.

Current year preliminary counts from the Maine Tracking Network show that health care providers reported over 5,000 cases of tickborne disease so far this year. This includes diseases like Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, and babesiosis.

“Many people think ticks are only a summer problem, but ticks can remain active throughout the fall,” said Maine CDC Director Puthiery Va. “You can enjoy Maine’s beautiful fall weather and outdoor activities while staying safe by taking a few simple steps before, during, and after can help protect you from tickborne disease.”

Ticks often live in wooded and brushy areas and areas with leaf litter. The Maine CDC encourages everyone to think TICKS when spending time outdoors: 

  • T – Take an EPA-approved repellent and use it before going outside. Use DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus on skin. Pre-treat clothing with permethrin.
  • I – Inspect your body daily. Check yourself, children, and pets for ticks after spending time outdoors.
  • C – Cover your skin. Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants and tuck pants into socks. Light-colored clothing makes ticks easier to spot.
  • K – Know your surroundings. Be aware when you are in tick habitat and take extra precautions.
  • S – Shower after being outdoors. Showering helps wash off ticks before they attach. Put clothes in the dryer on high heat for at least 15 minutes before washing to kill ticks.

Remember to check for ticks after any outdoor activity and before bed each night. Check in areas where ticks may be easy to miss, including the scalp, behind the ears, under the arms, around the waist, between the legs, and behind the knees.

The most common symptoms of tickborne disease include flu-like symptoms. People who have Lyme disease may also find an expanding rash somewhere on their body. This rash can sometimes, though not always, look like a bullseye. If you experience any of these symptoms, talk to a health care provider and be sure to mention any recent tick exposure.

The University of Maine Cooperative Extension Tick Lab offers tick identification for free and tick testing to Maine residents for a $20 fee. Testing can take up to three days and should be used for surveillance purposes only, not for diagnosis. Finding a tick on you, even if it was attached, does not necessarily mean that it spread any germs to you. Find more information at ticks.umaine.edu. 

To learn more about how to stay tick free, visit the Maine CDC's website.

AUGUSTA - Gov. Janet T. Mills has proclaimed October 2026 as National Disability Employment Awareness Month (NDEAM).

October 2026 marks the 81st anniversary of NDEAM. Gov. Mills' proclamation recognizes the contributions of people with disabilities to Maine's workplaces, communities and economy and calls on employers, schools, higher education institutions and community organizations to promote access to good, in-demand jobs and career pathways, including registered apprenticeship.

"At a time when employers are searching for workers, talented Maine people with disabilities are ready and willing to participate in the workforce," said Jennifer Kimble, the chair of Maine's Commission on Disability and Employment. "Expanding recruitment and retention strategies that recognize the value of including workers with disabilities as benefits businesses, communities, and the individuals whose talents are too often underutilized."

The Commission on Disability and Employment was established by the legislature in 1997 and promotes collaboration with the public and private sectors to increase awareness and influence policy related to employment for people with disabilities. Its members envision a Maine workforce that includes all people with disabilities employed in jobs that meet both their economic and personal needs.

"National Disability Employment Awareness Month is an opportunity to recognize the skills, talents and contributions of Mainers with disabilities and to continue working toward workplaces where everyone has the opportunity to contribute and succeed," said Maine Department of Labor Commissioner Laura Fortman. "Maine's workforce needs every person who wants to work, and the Department of Labor and our partners are committed to helping people with disabilities pursue meaningful careers while helping employers connect with talented workers."

NDEAM has been observed nationally since 1945. The observance recognizes the contributions of people with disabilities and promotes employment opportunities and career pathways.

items.title: Maine State Archives offers expanded digital access with Open Access — Maine Secretary of State — Bureau of Corporations, Elections & Commissions News
items.content_text:
AUGUSTA, MAINE
– Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today announced the official launch of Open Access, the Maine State Archives (MSA) new online platform for publicly accessible, digitized and born-digital public records. The platform can be accessed at
https://digitalarchives.maine.gov
or from the Maine State Archives section of the Secretary of State website.
Open Access is the public-facing side of a strategic effort to maintain a digital preservation system for records of Maine state government. The system ensures the long-term preservation and accessibility of state records that are archival or subject to long-term retention.
“From the beginning, I have been committed to improving efficiency and modernizing our systems to benefit Mainers and streamline access,” said
Secretary Bellows
. “Open Access will provide improved government transparency in a user-friendly platform that will be continuously expanded as more and more collections are imaged.”
Overall, MSA’s collections span five centuries from the 1639 royal land grant to Sir Ferdinand Gorges to the 2024 papers of the Lewiston Tragedy Commission. One section of the site is devoted to Maine history before statehood, highlighting important records such as Revolutionary War land grants and the Rolls and Rosters Book of Orders for the 8th Division of the Maine Militia. The records of Maine’s involvement in the Civil War are extensive. Open Access currently holds just over 100,000 imaged records so far.
“With more than 8 miles of documents in the Archives care, there is a long way to go to digitize them all, but it’s a great start,” said Maine State Archivist Christian Cotz. “We’re excited to continue to add records to the platform and provide Mainers from students to researchers with even more to discover each time they visit the site.”
###

items.title: US Department of Labor awards $10.2 million to 67 organizations to promote workplace safety and health training — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration today announced the award approximately $10.2 million in grant funds to 67 organizations across the nation to support education and training focused on worker safety to help employees and employers recognize serious workplace hazards and employ safety and health programs.Funded through the Susan Harwood Training Grant Program, the grants aim to advance worker safety and health by providing instructor-led training opportunities for workers and employers in small businesses with an emphasis on industries with high injury, illness, and fatality rates.The grants will fund training and education on hazard awareness, prevention, and controls to protect workers from on-the-job hazards through the development of quality classroom-ready training and educational materials that identify and prevent workplace hazards.The grants honor the legacy and work of Dr. Susan Harwood who, during her 17 years with OSHA, developed workplace safety guidelines for benzene, formaldehyde, bloodborne pathogens and lead in the construction industry. Harwood was also primary author of OSHA’s cotton dust standard which virtually eliminated byssinosis – a lung disease that causes asthma-like symptoms – among textile workers.Learn more about the Susan Harwood Training Grant Program and 2026 awardees.

items.title: US Labor Department finds railroad illegally terminated employee who refused to work during severe weather — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: LITTLE ROCK, AR – A U.S. Department of Labor Occupational Safety and Health Administration whistleblower investigation has concluded that Union Pacific Railroad Co. violated the Federal Railroad Safety Act when it removed from service and later terminated a North Little Rock yardman who notified management of nearby lightning and federal safety standards. OSHA determined that the employee voiced concerns about nearby lightning, cited OSHA and NOAA lightening safety guidelines, initiated a safety stand-down, and refused to work until the storm passed. Within minutes of the stand-down, Union Pacific removed the employee from service and was later charged with insubordination. Union Pacific terminated his employment on May 30, 2024.On June 10, 2026, OSHA ordered Union Pacific to remove from the employee’s employment records any reference of the incident, and pay back wages, lost benefits, compensatory and punitive damages totaling at least $304,869, and attorney’s fees. Union Pacific filed objections to OSHA’s order and has requested a hearing before a U.S. Department of Labor Administrative Law Judge.OSHA’s Whistleblower Protection Program enforces 25 whistleblower statutes that protect employees from retaliation for reporting violations of workplace airline, anti-money laundering, commercial motor carrier, consumer product, criminal antitrust, environmental, financial reform, food safety, health insurance reform, maritime, motor vehicle safety, nuclear, pipeline, public transportation agency, railroad, safety and health, securities, and tax laws.Editor’s note: The U.S. Department of Labor does not release the names of employees involved in whistleblower complaints.

items.title: General Provisions; Revised List of Birds Protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act — Federal Register — Documents Matching 'Maine'
items.content_text: We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), propose to revise the List of Birds Protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) by both adding and removing species and changing names to conform to accepted use by the scientific community. Reasons for the proposed changes to the list include adding species based on new taxonomy and new evidence of natural occurrence in the United States or U.S. territories, removing species no longer known to occur within the United States or U.S. territories, and changing names to reflect currently accepted taxonomy and nomenclature. The net increase of 25 species (32 added and 7 removed) would bring the total number of species protected by the MBTA to 1,131. We also propose to revise the names of species subject to specific migratory bird permit regulations to reflect currently accepted taxonomy and nomenclature. We are taking this proposed action because an accurate and up-to-date list of species protected by the MBTA is essential for public notification, regulatory, and law-enforcement purposes, and to ensure consistency in the use of common and scientific names across Service regulations.

Maine Forest Service report highlights effectiveness of forestry practices that protect water quality

October 1, 2026

AUGUSTA, Maine, October 1, 2026 - A new Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Maine Forest Service (MFS) report underscores the effectiveness of environmentally friendly practices during timber harvesting. Released Oct. 1, the "Maine Forestry Best Management Practices Use and Effectiveness Data Summary" draws on hundreds of observations at timber harvesting sites across Maine.

This MFS study shows how forestry and timber industry professionals use recommended practices statewide. It also demonstrates that the risk to waterbodies greatly increases when they are improperly applied.

These measures, called Best Management Practices (BMP), are voluntarily implemented by professionals to help protect water quality in Maine's streams, rivers, lakes, and wetlands. They cover planning and application recommendations for activities such as stream crossings, road construction, and controlling erosion and sediment, the primary pollutants associated with timber harvesting.

Maines forest industry has made great strides in protecting water resources in recent decades, said State Forester and MFS Director Patty Cormier. The improvements weve identified through our BMP monitoring program are a testament to the ongoing value of the training that loggers, foresters, and woodland owners have participated in and applied. We thank them, our training partners, and collaborators for their contributions to this progress.

The report, released every two years, is the result of this monitoring from 2024 to 2025. It includes data from 165 timber harvesting sites and observations on over 700 individual activities, including around stream crossings, contaminants, and log landing placement.

This year's key findings include:

  • 74% of study sites applied appropriate practices on stream crossings. In many cases, they included planning to avoid crossings altogether. MFS emphasizes avoiding stream crossings when possible because they present the highest risk for sedimentation.
  • Soil movement monitoring found that, in 85% of cases, no sediment entered a water body. Of the 15% instances where sediment was recorded, 9% were in measurable amounts (~1 cubic foot or more of sediment), and 6% were trace amounts.
  • 87% of sites showed no evidence of chemical spills, a 10% decrease from the previous report. Reported spills ranged from minor drips to less than 10 square feet.
  • Progress on improving fish passage continues. Although the number of stream-crossing structures adequately spanning stream channels on haul roads decreased by 5% since the previous report, adequate crossings on operation trails increased by 17%.

This year's results are largely consistent with previous reports and continue to show that Maine's forestry and logging communities are using BMPs effectively. BMP use and effectiveness at timber harvesting operations are monitored regularly by the MFS District Foresters and Water Resources Specialist. In addition, MFS staff provide regular training and support for their application, with presentations and workshops across the state.

Since 2000, MFS staff have conducted a systematic statewide monitoring program of BMPs on a sample of timber harvesting operations across the state. Support from Maine landowners, loggers, and foresters has been critical to its implementation and effectiveness. MFS efforts also include financial incentives for loggers and foresters to acquire temporary bridges, which are among the most effective measures to install stream crossings with minimal impact.

In the latest report, and throughout the programs history, monitoring shows that when sedimentation was observed, it was most often due to inadequate BMP application. The risk of detrimental impacts also greatly increases if they are not applied or applied incorrectly. Previous reports and numerous national studies have also documented that BMPs help protect water resources when properly applied. The latest findings reinforce that continued monitoring, education, and training are key to sustaining the success of forestry BMPs and their environmental benefits.

The report can be found on the MFS Forest Policy and Management Division website.

items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor today announced the award of $43 million in Industry-Driven Skills Training Fund grants to seven states to invest in employer-driven skills training programs for critical industries like shipbuilding, advanced manufacturing, and nuclear energy.Administered by the department’s Employment and Training Administration, the second round of Industry-Driven Skills Training Fund grants will provide funding to State Workforce Agencies to provide outcome-based reimbursements to employers who provide training that is responsive to rapidly evolving skill requirements and local workforce needs. More than $10 million of the awarded funding supports occupations in the domestic shipbuilding industry and the maritime supply chain.“President Trump is restoring American manufacturing dominance, especially in critical industries like manufacturing, shipbuilding, and nuclear energy," said Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. "As we continue to see growth in the construction and manufacturing sectors these grants ensure that American workers have the skills necessary to fill the high-skilled and high-paying jobs that are driving our nation into a new era of industrial might and provide the economic security that previous administrations let slip overseas.”In September 2025, the department awarded more than $86 million to 14 states in the first round of Industry-Driven Skills Training Fund grants. Across both rounds, the grants invest more than $129 million in 21 states nationwide, including over $30 million for the shipbuilding industry. These investments support the Administration’s reindustrialization agenda and its commitment to building the skilled workforce for high-growth and emerging industries including advanced manufacturing; aerospace; infrastructure; building and construction; cybersecurity; domestic mineral production; healthcare; information technology; maritime supply chain; nuclear energy; quantum computing; and shipbuilding

items.title: US Labor Department obtains court order naming independent fiduciary  for 401(k) plan of defunct WA-based aerospace company — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: SEATTLE – The U.S. Department of Labor has secured a court order to appoint an independent fiduciary to manage the abandoned 401(k) plan of a defunct Arlington-based aerospace company.The order, entered in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington, appoints AMI Benefit Plan Administrators Inc. as the independent fiduciary for the Commercial Aircraft Interiors LLC 401(k) Plan, which has been frozen since the employer shut down operations in 2023. In this role, the independent fiduciary will be able to distribute its assets to eligible former employees who have not been able to access their retirement savings because the only responsive company representative, Charles Pratt, lacked the legal authority needed to approve distributions. The independent fiduciary will also be able to formally terminate the plan.“The appointment of an independent fiduciary will give the participants in the Commercial Aircraft Interiors plan access to the funds that rightly belong to them,” said Liam Roberts, district director for the department’s Employee Benefits Security Administration in Seattle. “We urge all workers to contact the department for assistance when their retirement plan has been abandoned and they have not received the benefits to which they are entitled.”Under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, all employee benefit plans are required to be managed by named fiduciaries. items.content_html: WASHINGTON – The United States and Mexico today announced the successful resolution of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) facility-specific Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) matter regarding theAkwel Juárez México, S.A. de C.V. (Akwel or the company) facility located in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, Mexico. The United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation to address labor violations occurring at the facility, including employer interference in union activity and retaliatory dismissals of workers. That plan has now been implemented, and the denial of rights concerns raised in our request for review have been remediated. As a result, the United States Trade Representative has directed the Secretary of the Treasury to resume liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the facility.The measure marks genuine progress in safeguarding U.S. workers' ability to compete internationally, requiring Mexican producers to follow Mexican law and the terms of the USMCA. Actions taken during the course of remediation allowed the Akwel workers to elect a representative union and negotiate a collective bargaining agreement with improvements to wages and working conditions at the facility. This case represents another victory for the Trump Administration, whose America First policy prioritizes American workers by preventing foreign auto parts manufacturers from weakening worker protections to obtain an unfair trade advantage.The Department of Labor’s Bureau of International Labor Affairs and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative facilitated a resolution with the Government of Mexico (Mexico) to remediate workers’ claims at Akwel.Actions taken by the facility to address the matter include:Reinstating three workers with full backpay and benefits and paying full severance to six workers, based on their respective preferences; Restructuring human resources and labor relations management, and taking appropriate disciplinary action against staff who violated workers’ freedom of association and collective bargaining rights;Implementing and training all company personnel on its neutrality statement and guidelines related to freedom of association and collective bargaining, including a zero-tolerance policy for violations, and committing to retraining annually; Informing workers about the denial of rights at the facility by conducting meetings and posting notices at the facility to acknowledge Akwel’s unlawful and interfering practices and affirm the company’s intention to respect workers’ rights in the future;Installing and publicizing a complaint mechanism through which workers can report violations of their rights and breaches of company policies anonymously and confidentially; andMaintaining on the company website and in any internal communications platform the neutrality statement and guidelines, collective bargaining agreement, training materials, and information about complaint mechanisms maintained by the company and Mexico, such that the information is easily accessible to workers.Actions taken by Mexico to address the matter include:Monitoring the facility with regard to the obligations of the course of remediation and compliance with Mexican laws related to freedom of association and collective bargaining; Conducting in-person training that is structured to ensure all workers understand their right to freedom of association and collective bargaining and how to exercise it, including by informing workers of the denial of rights at the facility and educating workers on the conciliation process available to any dismissed worker;Conducting separate workers’ rights training for supervisors, human resources and labor relations personnel, and other high-level and “trusted” officials; Maintaining a direct email address, reporting platform, and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of freedom of association and collective bargaining rights, and timely investigate any allegations; and Imposing sanctions in accordance with Mexican law, including financial penalties, on Akwel for violating Mexican laws related to freedom of association and collective bargaining.BackgroundThe Secretary of Labor and the United States Trade Representative co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On October 24, 2024, the ILC received an RRM petition from Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores y Empleados Especializados, Conexos y Similares de la República Mexicana (SINATAM), a Mexican labor union, along with ten workers as signatories. The petition alleged Akwel had violated workers’ right to collective bargaining and freedom of association by refusing to negotiate a collective bargaining agreement with the petitioner union, dismissing workers based on their union affiliation, and threatening and harassing workers to disincentivize their union activity. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms. As a result, on November 22, 2024, the United States submitted a request that Mexico review the matter. Mexico agreed to conduct a review and, on January 6, 2025, concluded a denial of the rights had occurred at the facility. Subsequently, the United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation. The end date of the course of remediation was January 31, 2026. The United States closely monitored compliance with the course of remediation.Read the full course of remediation.Read an unofficial courtesy Spanish translation of the full course of remediation.Read the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury.Learn more about the department’s work to make global competition fair for American workers.

Supreme Judicial Court to Hold Oral Arguments at Three Maine High Schools

Date: 9/29/2026

The Supreme Judicial Court will hold court and hear a total of nine cases at three Maine high schools next week.

On Tuesday, October 6, beginning at 9:00 a.m., the Court will visit Katahdin Middle/High School in Stacyville to hear arguments in three appellate cases. Senator Trey Stewart extended the invitation to the Law Court. The three cases are scheduled to begin at 9:00 a.m., 10:00 a.m., and 11:00 a.m.

The Court will hear three appeals at Morse High School in Bath on Wednesday, October 7 at the invitation of Senator Denise Tepler. The Court will follow the same schedule with the first oral argument starting at 9:00 a.m., the second at 10:00 a.m., and the third at 11:00 a.m.

And on Thursday, October 8, the Court will hear three cases at Kennebunk High School at the invitation of Representative Daniel Sayre. Again, the schedule indicates that the first case starts at 9:00 a.m.

Students receive copies of the briefs in advance and, after each argument, the lawyers stay to answer questions from interested students. When the cases are decided, the schools receive a link to the decisions to share with the students.

Beginning in 2005, the Court has held oral arguments in actual appellate cases at over 40 Maine high schools around the state. In each school, the gymnasium, cafeteria, or auditorium is turned into a courtroom for the morning so that the students can observe the appellate process. The Court has visited schools from York County to Aroostook County; from Oxford County to Washington County; and many places in between.

Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill said, "We hope that providing real-time exposure to the third branch of government supplements the students' civics education and exposes Maine learners to the concept of justice. The practice of appellate law is rarely seen on television or in the movies. Creating a courtroom environment in a high school takes great effort on the part of the school administration and staff and we appreciate their extensive efforts."

The press is welcome to attend. The case schedule has been posted on the Courts website here.

Live video streaming of these cases, and all other Supreme Judicial Court oral arguments, is available here.

If interviews or photographs are desired while the Court is at the schools, please contact Julie Finn beforehand to schedule an interview at the below email address. Photographs and video of students are subject to the rules of the high school, and the press is requested to contact school officials directly.

Contact: Julia Finn, Esq.
Phone: (207) 822-0767 (office)

Up in the mountains of Montenegro, among the chatter of many nations, I listened to dignitaries and servicemembers comment on the success of the day, on the readiness for the mission, and on the grit and pride of that international team.

My thoughts turned to Shakespeare, a bard of some four centuries ago, who could not have envisioned the future circumstances which we find ourselves in today, but who said prophetically and for all time: "the Readiness is all."

Readiness indeed. Readiness is what I saw in Montenegro last week. Readiness for things known and unknown, unexpected and expected.

I traveled there with Major General Diane Dunn and Maine National Guardsmen to Montenegro to observe that joint training mission and to meet with Montenegrin officials, military members, and citizens to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Maine's strategic partnership with Montenegro. I am the second governor to have visited Montenegro and celebrate this partnership.

In 2006, Maine and Montenegro formed that partnership to share training and military expertise, as Montenegro became a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO. Both the state of Maine and the people of Montenegro have benefited through this shared knowledge, through team exercises, and through progress in this strategic partnership.

Over the past 20 years, our servicemembers and Montenegrins have trained side-by-side, shoulder-to-shoulder, learning how to navigate challenging mountain terrain, practicing difficult search and rescue missions, confronting dangerously cold weather conditions, and defending the security of our respective regions. Montenegrin soldiers have traveled to Maine for engineering projects, and Maine National Guardsmen have traveled to Montenegro to respond to cyber-attacks on that country. 

While in Montenegro, Major General Dunn and I met with the Prime Minister and the President, Defense Minister, and Foreign Minister of the country to discuss the future of our relationship and the prospects for more collaboration. Collaboration in forestry research, in deep port uses, in trade, and in educational exchanges for the benefit of both regions.

Maine, like Montenegro, for instance, has a deep ocean port, which is an important gateway for trade. We are tackling threats of cybersecurity and threats from severe weather caused by climate change, just as they are. We too have a thriving forest products industry that is at the heart of our economy.

So I emphasized to the Montenegrins that Maine offers world-leading universities, community colleges, and private higher eds, who are all ready to work with Montenegro students to train the next generation of best and brightest leaders—broadening research and bolstering our mutual security.

I am proud of our own Guard members and of their determination to reach outside their own boundaries and zones of operation and zones of comfort to assist the people of Montenegro in addressing cybersecurity threats, in training and in military preparedness, and in maximizing the potential for international collaboration and expertise.

To properly commemorate the 20th anniversary of this bilateral commitment of the Maine National Guard and the Armed Forces of Montenegro, I've officially proclaimed September 17th as Montenegro-Maine Partnership Day, reaffirming our friendship with the leaders, the people, and the Armed Forces of Montenegro.

Maine and Montenegro have contributed our human and physical resources to this effort, and our culture, our character, and our courage have combined for the common good of humanity and for the common peace of our nations.

Maine and Montenegro are ready.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and I thank you for listening.

The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) reminds Maine people and visitors to take steps to keep themselves, their loved ones, and neighbors healthy this respiratory virus season.

Respiratory viruses can cause fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle aches, and fatigue. Some people are more likely to get very sick and need medical attention. These viruses can spread when an infected person coughs or sneezes. They can also spread from touching the surface with the virus on it and then touching your nose or mouth before washing your hands.

The Maine CDC recommends the following measures to protect yourself and others:

  • Stay home when you are sick.
  • Wash your hands frequently with soap and water.
  • Clean and disinfect surfaces and objects that people touch often.
  • If you are sick, consider wearing a mask around others.
  • Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow.
  • Avoid close contact with people who are sick.
  • Get vaccinated, as appropriate for flu, COVID-19, and RSV.

Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent respiratory viruses. Vaccines can also help make illness less severe and help prevent missed work or school. Getting a flu vaccine every year and staying up to date with COVID-19 and RSV vaccinations, if eligible, can help lower the risk of getting sick.

Consistent with the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the Maine CDC recommends the following respiratory virus immunization for the 2026-2027 season:

  • Flu: Everyone 6 months and older should receive an annual flu vaccine.
  • COVID-19: Vaccination is recommended for
    • all children ages 6 through 23 months;
    • children and adolescents ages 2 through 18 years who are at increased risk for severe COVID-19 or who want to be vaccinated;
    • adults age 19 and older;
    • pregnant individuals.
  • RSV: Immunization is recommended for certain infants, pregnant people, and older adults.
    • Infants: RSV immunization is recommended for those younger than 8 months born during or entering their first RSV season, if they are not protected by maternal RSV vaccination.
      • Certain children ages 8-19 months who are at increased risk for severe RSV may also be recommended to receive RSV immunization during their second season.
    • Pregnant people: RSV vaccination is recommended during weeks 32 through 36 of pregnancy.
    • Older adults: All adults age 75 and older and adults 50-74 at increased risk for severe RSV illness.

To find the nearest location to get a vaccine, contact your local pharmacy or health care provider.
